nameStory: The name 'hollyhock' comes from the old English word 'holyoke,' given by 16th-century herbalist William Turner. This garden favorite earned its holy association because pilgrims and crusaders carried the seeds along sacred routes, spreading these towering beauties across Europe from their original home in China.
description: Hollyhocks are tall, stately garden plants that can reach 6-8 feet high, creating living walls of colorful flowers. These old-fashioned favorites produce large, papery blooms that spiral up sturdy stems from bottom to top throughout summer. The flowers come in many colors including pink, red, white, yellow, and deep purple, each bloom measuring 3-4 inches across. Though originally from China, they've become beloved cottage garden classics that often self-seed and return year after year.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, papery flowers with 5 broad petals arranged in a simple, open cup shape. The petals feel delicate and slightly crinkled, like tissue paper, and surround a prominent central column of fuzzy stamens that stick out noticeably.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall spikes that shoot up 6-8 feet high with flowers arranged spirally up the stem. The plants start blooming at the bottom and work their way up over several weeks, creating a tower effect.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with slightly fuzzy surfaces that feel soft to touch. The leaves have shallow, rounded lobes and are arranged alternately up the stem, getting smaller toward the top.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, round seed pods that split into segments like orange slices when ripe. Each 'slice' contains one kidney-shaped seed and feels papery when dry.

habitat: Hollyhocks thrive in sunny garden spots with well-drained soil, often found along cottage garden borders, fence lines, and house foundations. In New England, look for them in established gardens, old farmsteads, and sometimes as garden escapes in disturbed areas near homes. They prefer full sun but can tolerate some afternoon shade.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves in a low rosette. Plants focus on building strong root systems and leafy growth during cool spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from July through August, with tall flower spikes reaching full height. Flowers open progressively from bottom to top of each spike.
seasonality.fall: Upper flowers may continue blooming into early fall while lower flowers develop into distinctive round, segmented seed pods. Leaves begin to yellow and decline.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level, leaving dried stalks with persistent seed pods. Seeds scatter during winter storms, often sprouting nearby the following spring.

funFact: Hollyhock flowers are completely edible and have a mild, sweet taste - Victorian children used to make 'dolls' by inverting the blooms and using the bud as a head, while modern chefs use the colorful petals to garnish salads and make floral ice cubes.
confusionNotes: Hollyhocks are sometimes confused with wild mallows, but hollyhocks are much taller (6-8 feet vs 1-3 feet) and have much larger flowers. Remember: 'High hollyhocks, low mallows' - if you're looking up at the flowers, it's probably a hollyhock.
contextualKnowledge: Though often called 'old-fashioned' flowers, hollyhocks were actually exotic imports that became so beloved they seem native to New England gardens. Many people don't realize these cottage garden staples originally traveled the ancient Silk Road from China centuries ago.
compareHints: Hollyhocks are the only member of the Alcea genus commonly found in New England gardens. They're most similar to other mallow family members like wild mallow and rose-of-Sharon, but dwarf both in size and flower magnitude. Unlike their smaller mallow cousins, hollyhocks create dramatic vertical displays that can tower over garden visitors.
